title: Pair Everyone So That Nobody Wants to Elope

concept.title: Proposals and engagements: the Gale-Shapley algorithm
body: There are `n` men and `n` women, and everybody ranks all the people of the other group. A pairing is **stable** if there is no man and woman who are not together but both prefer each other to their own partners (such a pair would elope). It is a surprising fact that a stable pairing **always exists**, and a simple procedure finds one. Several stable pairings can exist; the procedure below finds the one that is best for the men, which is unique, so it is a good thing to print.

The *Gale-Shapley algorithm* is a sequence of proposals. While a man is free, he proposes to the best woman on his list **to whom he has not yet proposed**. A free woman accepts. A woman who is engaged compares the new man with her fiance and keeps the one she likes more; the other becomes free again. Nobody ever proposes twice to the same woman, so there are at most `n * n` proposals.

Why does it end with everybody engaged and nobody eloping? A woman's partner only gets better over time, and a man only moves down his list. If a man `m` and a woman `w` preferred each other, then `m` must have proposed to `w` before (she is higher on his list than his final partner), and `w` rejected him or dropped him for someone she likes more, so her final partner is better than `m` in her eyes. The order in which free men are picked does not change the result. Print, for every man, the woman he ends up with.

statement: There are `n` men and `n` women, numbered 1 to n, and everybody has a strict ranking of all the people of the other group. A pairing of every man with a different woman is stable if there is no man and woman, not paired with each other, who both prefer the other to their own partner. Among all stable pairings print the one that is best for the men (every man gets the best woman he can get in any stable pairing; this pairing is unique).
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of men and the number of women.
The next `n` lines describe the men: line `i` lists all the women (numbers 1 to n) in the order in which the man `i` likes them, best first.
The next `n` lines describe the women: line `j` lists all the men in the order in which the woman `j` likes them, best first.
outputFormat: Print `n` numbers on one line: for each man from 1 to n, the woman he is paired with.
constraints: Every line is a permutation of the numbers 1 to n.

examples.note: Each man gets his first choice (the man 1 the woman 1, the man 2 the woman 2), so no man wants to leave, and the pairing is stable: 1 2.
Both men want the woman 1, and she prefers the man 2: he gets her, and the man 1 gets the woman 2: 2 1.

hints: A free man proposes to the next woman on his list; he never proposes to the same woman twice.
A woman keeps the man she prefers, using a table of her ranking of each man.
Repeat until no man is free, then print the partner of every man.

explanation: Free men propose in the order of their lists; a woman keeps the better of her fiance and the new proposer, and the loser becomes free again. Nobody proposes twice to the same woman, so there are at most n * n proposals; the result is the pairing that is best for the men.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
men = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]
women = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

rank = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
for w in range(1, n + 1):
    for position, m in enumerate(women[w - 1]):
        rank[w][m] = position
nxt = [0] * (n + 1)
partner = [0] * (n + 1)
free = list(range(n, 0, -1))
while free:
    m = free.pop()
    w = men[m - 1][nxt[m]]
    nxt[m] += 1
    if partner[w] == 0:
        partner[w] = m
    elif rank[w][m] < rank[w][partner[w]]:
        free.append(partner[w])
        partner[w] = m
    else:
        free.append(m)
wife = [0] * (n + 1)
for w in range(1, n + 1):
    wife[partner[w]] = w
print(*wife[1:])
